A crest means the highest point of something — the very top, the peak, the part that rises above everything else around it. Almost every meaning of this word connects back to this single idea of topmost-ness.

1. The top of a hill, mountain, or wave

This is the most literal use. The crest of a hill is the very highest line of that hill — the ridge at the top, where the ground stops going up and starts going down. The crest of a wave is that curling, foamy top edge of a wave just before it crashes.

"The hikers finally reached the crest of the hill and saw the valley below."
"The surfer rode just below the crest of the wave."

Think of it this way: if you drew a hill on paper, put your finger on the very tippy-top — that's the crest.

2. The tuft of feathers (or fur/skin) on top of an animal's head

Some animals have a natural decoration that stands up on the top of their head. This raised tuft, fan, or spike of feathers, fur, or skin is called a crest. It literally sits at the "top" of the animal, which connects back to the core idea.

You've likely seen this on:

  • A cockatoo — the fan of feathers it raises on top of its head
  • A hoopoe bird — a striking fan of orange and black feathers on its head
  • A rooster (cock) — the red fleshy comb/ridge on top of its head
  • A crested gecko — the little ridges running along the top of its head

"The cockatoo raised its crest when it felt threatened."

3. A heraldic symbol or family/institutional emblem

This is a very common use in everyday life. A crest here means a special design or symbol that officially represents a family, school, sports team, military regiment, company, or city.

You see these on:

  • School uniforms (the logo/badge on the blazer pocket)
  • Football club shirts
  • Official letterheads and certificates
  • Rings and shields

"The students wore a blazer with the school's crest on the breast pocket."
"The knight's shield bore his family crest."

Why is it called a crest? In medieval times, knights wore armour, and on top of their helmet, they fixed a decorative three-dimensional figure (like a lion, an eagle, or a plume of feathers). This figure sat at the very top of the helmet — the highest point — and was called the crest. Over time, the word came to describe the whole symbolic emblem of a family or group, even without the helmet.

So a "family crest" is basically the inherited symbol of a family — a visual identity passed down through generations.

4. The top of a helmet (in armour/heraldry)

Closely related to the point above, and worth knowing separately: in the context of historical armour and heraldry (the formal system of symbols used by noble families), the crest specifically refers to the decorative figure mounted on the very top of a knight's helmet. It was purely the piece on top — not the whole coat of arms.

"The knight's crest was a golden lion standing on top of his helmet."

5. A ridge on a bone (in anatomy)

In medicine and biology, the word crest is used for a narrow, raised ridge on a bone — because it resembles the ridge/peak shape of a hill's crest.

The most commonly mentioned one is the iliac crest — the curved bony ridge you can feel at the top of your hip. Run your hand along your side down to your hip, and that hard ridge you feel is the iliac crest.

"The doctor located the iliac crest to guide the injection."

Because "crest" means "the highest point," it is also used figuratively to mean the peak of an achievement, emotion, or situation — the moment when something is at its greatest height.

"She was at the crest of her career when the award was announced."
"The team was riding the crest of a wave of good form." (This phrase — "riding the crest of a wave" — is a very common idiom meaning to be enjoying a period of great success or good fortune.)

It helps to see that every single use of "crest" shares one unifying thread:

UseWhat sits at the "top"?

In every case, the crest is the thing that is uppermost:

  • On a landscape → it's the top of the hill
  • On a wave → it's the top curl of water
  • On an animal → it's the tuft on top of the head
  • On a helmet → it's the decoration on top
  • On a bone → it's the raised ridge on the surface
  • On a family's identity → it's the emblem that "crowns" them
  • In life → it's the peak of success or a situation

Once you lock in that core idea — the topmost, highest, or most prominent point of something — every use of this word will make immediate sense to you, no matter the context.
